tools.title: Pattern language for messaging integration
tools.definition: The book presents 65 patterns as an interlinked language: each pattern names a recurring design decision and points to the patterns that follow from it, so a design is composed by walking the language rather than by picking isolated recipes.

hooks.clause: a pattern language is a vocabulary for planning passes: name the decision, the forces, and the next decision it opens

tools.title: Business criticality of integration
tools.definition: Once applications depend on it, the integration layer is mission-critical; its failures cost real money, which raises the bar for reliability and operations.

place.chapter: Chapter 1: Solving Integration Problems Using Patterns

tools.title: Predictive router vs reactive filtering

transform.reason: No destination predicate set or duplicate-traffic cost function is supplied.

observable: Routing knowledge shifts between a hub and recipient units.

tools.definition: A content-based router decides up front and must know every destination (predictive); the alternative broadcasts on a publish-subscribe channel and lets each receiver filter (reactive), trading sender knowledge and single-point maintenance against duplicate traffic and receiver-side rules.

hooks.clause: hooks that each decide what they handle are reactive filtering; the harness router is predictive; mixing both needs a stated rule

verified.note: model-knowledge (the site excerpts of both patterns omit the comparison)

tools.title: Message Filter

observable: Only messages whose numeric selector meets the threshold continue.

tools.definition: A router with one output channel: messages matching a condition pass through, the rest are dropped, so a component never receives traffic it does not care about.

hooks.clause: UIFA roles see a filtered record stream, not the whole log
each hook filters the events it handles and drops the rest

tools.title: Stateless vs stateful filters (duplicate elimination)
tools.definition: Most filters judge each message alone, but a filter that drops duplicates or applies a quota must remember what it has seen, which makes it stateful and harder to replicate.

hooks.clause: duplicate receipts need a stateful filter keyed by id before projection

tools.title: Dynamic Router

transform.reason: No registration messages, matching predicates, or conflict resolution rule is defined.

observable: Recipient announcements change later routing decisions.

tools.definition: A router that configures itself: potential recipients announce on a control channel the conditions under which they can handle a message, the router stores these in a rule base, and each message goes to the recipient whose rules match, so the router need not be maintained per recipient.

hooks.clause: registered targets announce what they accept on a control record; publication routes from the announcements
worker roles announce their capabilities; the dispatcher routes by rule base rather than hard-coded role lists

tools.title: Dynamic router trade-offs: rule conflicts, rule-base upkeep, recipient participation

transform.reason: No matching-rule representation or priority tie-break contract is supplied.

observable: A message may match several recipient registrations.

tools.definition: Self-configuration removes router maintenance but requires every recipient to speak the control protocol, needs a policy when several recipients' rules match (first, all, priority), and makes the effective routing harder to read because it lives in runtime state rather than configuration.

hooks.clause: if hooks self-register, record the rule base so the effective routing stays inspectable

tools.title: Recipient List

observable: A message reaches every member of a numbered recipient set.

tools.definition: A router that computes, per message, the set of recipients and forwards a copy to each one's channel, normally unchanged; the list may derive from message data (an order's value sets how many agencies are asked) or from preferences.

hooks.clause: fan-out to a computed set of workers is a recipient list; record the list with the dispatch
publication to registered targets is a recipient list computed per release

tools.title: Recipient list variants: static vs dynamic; list from content, configuration or subscriptions

transform.reason: No content-to-list or subscription-to-list computation is specified.

observable: The chosen recipient set changes with its source of knowledge.

tools.definition: The recipient set may be fixed in configuration, derived from the message, or built from recipients' own subscription requests (the dynamic recipient list), moving the knowledge from sender to configuration to recipients respectively.

hooks.clause: targets that subscribe themselves versus a release list the operator edits: pick and name the source of truth

verified.note: eip-site:RecipientList.html (content-derived examples); model-knowledge (static, configuration, subscription variants)

tools.title: Robust delivery to every recipient: transactional send or idempotent receivers

transform.reason: No atomic multi-send transaction or receiver effect contract is defined.

observable: Partial fan-out leaves a mixture of reached and unreached units.

tools.definition: Sending to several channels is not atomic; either wrap the sends in one transaction so all or none are published, or accept partial sends and resend, which requires recipients to ignore duplicates.

hooks.clause: publication to many targets will partially fail; make target-side application idempotent and record what was delivered

verified.note: model-knowledge (the site excerpt lists Idempotent Receiver as related but does not explain)

tools.title: Splitter

transform.reason: No payload element selection and fragmentation transform is defined.

observable: A composite request yields independently processed part messages.

tools.definition: Breaks a composite message (an order with many line items) into one message per element or subset so each can be handled separately; the parts usually carry sequence or correlation data so an aggregator can reassemble them.

hooks.clause: intake mining splits a source into canonical units that carry their source locator for later reassembly
an order split into worker tasks is a splitter; tag parts with the order id and position

tools.title: Iterating vs static splitter; parts carry sequence and correlation

transform.reason: No composite payload schema or fragment metadata writer is available.

observable: Different split rules produce different numbered part sets.

tools.definition: A static splitter cuts a message into a known set of fixed parts; an iterating splitter walks a repeating element and emits one message per occurrence; in both cases each part should carry a set id, position and total so downstream aggregation knows when it is complete.

tools.title: Limited control over endpoints
tools.definition: Legacy and packaged applications usually cannot be changed, so the integration must work around their shortcomings at the edges rather than fixing them inside.

place.chapter: Chapter 1: Solving Integration Problems Using Patterns

hooks.clause: registered targets and constrained managed hosts cannot be changed; adapt at the kit edge

tools.title: Aggregator

transform.reason: No correlated-set state and payload merge transform exists.

observable: Related unit replies become one combined result.

tools.definition: A stateful filter that collects related messages (after a splitter or recipient list has fanned them out), holds them until the set is complete, and publishes one message built from them; it is defined by three decisions: correlation, completeness condition, aggregation algorithm.

hooks.clause: merging fan-out worker results into one verdict is an aggregator; name its correlation, completeness and algorithm
a refutation pass aggregates independent judgments; the completeness rule is a product decision

tools.title: Aggregator design decisions: correlation, completeness condition, aggregation algorithm

transform.reason: Correlation, completion, and merge rules each need an executable contract.

observable: Alternative reply groups close with different combined results.

tools.definition: Which incoming messages belong together (correlation), when the aggregate is ready to publish (completeness), and how the members are merged into one result (algorithm) are independent choices that together specify any aggregator.

hooks.clause: a fan-out brief should state all three before the first worker starts

tools.title: Completeness: wait for all

transform.reason: A correlated reply-set model and merged-result operation are missing.

observable: A result remains unavailable while any expected reply is missing.

tools.definition: Publish only when every expected member has arrived; the best-informed result but the slowest and most brittle, since one missing or late message blocks the aggregate, so a timeout must still raise an error.

hooks.clause: an operator waiting for every worker inherits the slowest; pair wait-for-all with an error timeout

tools.title: Completeness: timeout

transform.reason: The toy lacks a correlated reply set and partial-result merge rule.

observable: A deadline closes a reply set with only the arrivals received so far.

tools.definition: Wait a fixed time and decide with whatever has arrived; if nothing arrived, report an exception or retry; suited to scored bidding where any answer beats none.

hooks.clause: time budgets as the completeness rule for fan-out: decide at the deadline with what came back and record who was missing

tools.title: Completeness: first best

transform.reason: No acceptance predicate or correlated-set completion state is specified.

observable: One acceptable reply ends the wait and excludes later candidates.

tools.definition: Take the first acceptable response and ignore the rest; fastest, but discards information and gives late responders no influence.

hooks.clause: racing workers and taking the first answer trades thoroughness for latency; say so in the brief

tools.title: Completeness: timeout with override

transform.reason: No reply scoring, correlated-set state, or final-result selection contract is defined.

observable: A strong early answer ends the wait before its deadline.

tools.definition: Stop early as soon as a response meets a preset threshold; otherwise wait until the deadline and rank what arrived; combines the speed of first-best with the safety of a timeout.

hooks.clause: a refutation that finds a decisive counterexample can close the pass early; otherwise wait for the deadline

tools.title: Completeness: external event

transform.reason: No control-event vocabulary or aggregate completion state is available.

observable: A control event closes the currently collected reply set.

tools.definition: Close the aggregate when a business event arrives (end of trading day), typically an event message on a control channel, which gives central control over when sets complete.

hooks.clause: an operator phrase on the control channel closes an open aggregate (a planning pass, a review round)

tools.title: Aggregation strategies: select the best answer, condense data, collect for later evaluation

transform.reason: No reply payload schema, score function, or reduction transform is supplied.

observable: The same reply set can yield a winner, summary, or collection.

tools.definition: Three merge algorithms: pick one member by a scoring rule (best quote), reduce members to a summary (averages, totals, a merged document), or simply concatenate members into one message for a downstream decision maker.

hooks.clause: state whether worker results are ranked, condensed or collected; each needs a different handback shape
the idea ledger collects; synthesis condenses; a decision selects

verified.note: model-knowledge (the site excerpt names no strategy list; its bidding examples imply selection)

tools.title: Aggregate initialisation: by first member vs by a separate initialising message; known vs unknown expected count

transform.reason: No aggregate creation state and expected-member metadata contract is defined.

observable: A reply set starts with known or unknown membership.

tools.definition: An aggregate can start when its first member arrives or when a dedicated message from the splitter or recipient list announces the set and its size; knowing the expected count (from the splitter, the recipient list, or the auction's open set) decides which completeness conditions are even possible.

hooks.clause: write the dispatch record (set id, expected count) before the first worker returns so the aggregator can judge completeness

verified.note: model-knowledge; eip-site:BroadcastAggregate.html (known vs runtime-computed count affects completeness)

tools.title: Aggregator state, persistence, scaling and late arrivals

transform.reason: No persistent aggregate partition or late-member handling contract is supplied.

observable: Replies contend for shared sets and may arrive after closure.

tools.definition: Because it holds members until completion, an aggregator must persist state to survive a crash, cannot be freely replicated unless partitioned by correlation key (write contention appears when several members of one set land together), and must decide what to do with a member that arrives after its set was published.

hooks.clause: keep open aggregates as records in the log so a crashed aggregator resumes; log late arrivals rather than dropping them

verified.note: model-knowledge; eip-site:Aggregator.html (stateful; cloud examples retry on write contention)

tools.title: Few standards, vendor extensions
tools.definition: Integration standards fragment as vendors add extensions, so interoperability is weaker than the standards promise (the chapter recalls CORBA's experience).

tools.title: Resequencer

observable: Buffered messages leave in consecutive order after reordered arrival.

tools.definition: A stateful filter that collects messages arriving out of order (because related messages took different routes or ran in parallel) and republishes them in the required sequence over an order-preserving channel, normally without changing their content.

hooks.clause: projections over an append-only log must reorder records by sequence when writers raced; the log needs sequence numbers
worker returns arrive in any order; a resequencer restores dispatch order before a sequential consumer

tools.title: Sequence numbering requirements
tools.definition: Reordering needs a strictly consecutive, gap-free sequence (or a known expected set) assigned at the source, usually by the splitter or sender; without it the resequencer cannot know whether a gap is a missing message or the end.

hooks.clause: assign gap-free sequence numbers at the single writer; gaps then mean loss, not ambiguity

verified.note: model-knowledge (the site excerpt does not explain sequence assignment)

tools.title: Buffer overflow and unbounded buffers

transform.reason: No overflow choice is selected among blocking, dropping, and failing.

observable: A missing early message lets later messages fill the buffer.

tools.definition: While one early message is missing every later message must be held, so the buffer can grow without bound and exhaust memory; the resequencer therefore needs a capacity limit and a policy for what happens when it is reached.

hooks.clause: one worker that never returns holds every later result hostage; bound the buffer and surface the gap

verified.note: model-knowledge (book-only; the site excerpt mentions only an internal buffer)

tools.title: Throttling by active acknowledgment

observable: A sender cannot advance more than the allowed window beyond acknowledged progress.

tools.definition: Bound the buffer by flow control: the resequencer acknowledges to producers how far it has advanced and producers send only a window ahead, so at most a window's worth of messages can ever be buffered.

hooks.clause: budgets and subagent caps are a window; admit new fan-out only as earlier results are consumed

tools.title: Buffer persistence

transform.reason: No durable buffer, crash recovery, or transactional consume model is available.

observable: Buffered messages remain recoverable after a consumer failure.

tools.definition: Because buffered messages have been consumed from the input channel, a crash would lose them unless the buffer itself is durable or the consumption is transactional; a persistent buffer trades throughput for safety.

hooks.clause: held records belong in the log, not in a process's memory

tools.title: Missing messages: wait, stand-in, or skip after timeout

transform.reason: No stand-in payload or policy choice between waiting, replacement, and skipping is supplied.

observable: A sequence gap blocks, is replaced, or is skipped under a chosen rule.

tools.definition: When a sequence number never arrives the resequencer can block forever, insert a stand-in message so downstream can proceed, or skip the gap after a timeout and report it; each changes what downstream may assume.

hooks.clause: a missing worker result should become an explicit stand-in record so the aggregate can proceed and the gap stays visible

tools.title: Composed Message Processor

transform.reason: Payload splitting and merged-result construction are outside the closed transforms.

observable: Part results return as one response to the original unit.

tools.definition: One unit that splits a composite message, routes each part to the right processor, and re-aggregates the results into a single message, keeping the outer flow unaware that fan-out happened inside.

hooks.clause: fan an order's items out to specialised workers and merge: the caller sees one request and one reply

tools.title: Scatter-Gather

transform.reason: No reply correlation and result-aggregation transform is defined.

observable: Several unit answers contribute to one requester result.

tools.definition: Send one request to several recipients and use an aggregator to combine their replies into a single response; essentially a fan-out step followed by an aggregator, used when the same request should be answered by many parties (quotes, bids).

hooks.clause: the same brief to several workers with a merge is scatter-gather; it is the shape of refutation and adversarial review

tools.title: Distribution (recipient list) vs auction (publish-subscribe) variants

transform.reason: No reply membership and completion comparison model is supplied.

observable: Expected reply counts differ between addressed and open requests.

tools.definition: Distribution picks and addresses recipients, giving control and a known reply count (so wait-for-all is natural) but requiring knowledge of every recipient; auction broadcasts on one channel so any interested party may answer, needing only one channel but giving up control and leaving the reply count open, which forces timeout-style completeness.

hooks.clause: named workers (distribution) versus an open call any resident may answer (auction) decide the aggregator's completeness rule

tools.title: Routing Slip

transform.reason: Numeric parameters cannot encode an ordered route list and its per-message cursor.

observable: Each message follows its own precomputed processing route.

tools.definition: When the sequence of processing steps varies per message but is knowable up front, a component at the start computes the step list and attaches it to the message; each step, wrapped in a router, reads the slip after processing and forwards to the next step.

hooks.clause: the role chain executor, verifier, reviewer, release-close is a slip attached to the order when the chain is fixed per order kind

tools.title: Semantic differences
tools.definition: A shared syntax such as XML does not give shared meaning: the same field name (an account, a customer) denotes different things in different systems, and the gap must be bridged explicitly.

place.chapter: Chapter 1: Solving Integration Problems Using Patterns

hooks.clause: the feedback compiler must normalise meaning across sources, not only format

tools.title: Routing slip limits and strengths

transform.reason: No per-message itinerary representation or branching comparison is defined.

observable: Fixed routes avoid central state but cannot follow intermediate results.

tools.definition: Strengths: no central state, the route travels with the message, simple components; limits: strictly linear (no branching, loops or parallel legs), the route is fixed when the slip is written so intermediate results cannot change it, every step must understand the slip format, and a message in flight is hard to locate.

hooks.clause: a repair loop (resume: fix) is a branch the slip cannot express; that is the point where lifecycle state must live somewhere central

verified.note: model-knowledge (the site excerpt stops before limitations); eip-site:ProcessManager.html (slip assumed fixed and linear)

tools.title: Process Manager

transform.reason: No process-instance state machine or result-dependent transition graph is defined.

observable: A central unit advances several concurrent multi-step tasks.

tools.definition: A central component that holds the state of a multi-step process: a trigger message starts an instance, the manager sends work to a step, receives the reply, decides the next step from results so far, and repeats (hub-and-spoke), supporting branching, loops and parallel legs that a slip cannot.

hooks.clause: the lifecycle with repair loops and gates is process-manager shaped; today the operator's dispatch phrases are the manager
a resident holding lifecycle state would move the manager role from the operator's attention to a record

tools.title: Process definition vs process instance; correlating replies to the instance
tools.definition: The manager separates the template of steps (definition) from each running occurrence (instance, one per trigger); replies must carry a correlation id so the manager can resume the right instance, and instance state must be stored between steps.

hooks.clause: a role skill is the definition; a work order's run is the instance; every receipt must name the order it resumes

verified.note: eip-site:ProcessManager.html (per-trigger run, state, correlation link); model-knowledge (definition/instance terms)

tools.title: Process manager vs routing slip

transform.reason: No process graph, carried-route representation, or state cost model is specified.

observable: Task paths and central state differ between two coordination styles.

tools.definition: The slip is simpler and keeps no central state but only handles a route fixed up front and linear; the manager handles dynamic, branching and parallel flows and gives one place to see where each instance is, at the cost of a central hub that can bottleneck, must persist state, and is overkill for simple flows.

hooks.clause: choose per order kind: fixed chains as slips, chains with repair or parallel verification as managed instances

tools.title: Hub risks: bottleneck, single point of control, state persistence and recovery

transform.reason: No service capacity or durable process recovery model is supplied.

observable: A central coordinator delays or blocks unit task progress.

tools.definition: All traffic passes the hub, so throughput is bounded by it and a failure stops every instance; instance state must therefore be persisted (often as a document per instance) so a restarted manager resumes, and the manager should not be used where a simpler router suffices.

hooks.clause: lifecycle state persisted as records per order lets any session resume the process; the control log is that store

verified.note: eip-site:ProcessManager.html (bottleneck, single point of control, overkill); model-knowledge (persistence detail)

tools.title: Message Broker

transform.reason: A full broker topology and destination-rule contract are required beyond one policy.

observable: Unit traffic passes through a shared destination-selecting hub.

tools.definition: An architectural pattern: a central hub receives messages from many sources, determines each destination with the chapter's routing patterns, and forwards it, so senders are decoupled from receivers while flow stays centrally controlled (hub-and-spoke at the scale of the whole solution).

hooks.clause: the harness is the broker for records between roles, hosts and the console

tools.title: Broker trade-offs: bottleneck, complexity, broker hierarchy

transform.reason: No hierarchical topology mutation or broker service-time model is supplied.

observable: Traffic and routing state spread across multiple hubs.

tools.definition: One broker bounds throughput (mitigated by running stateless instances fed from a point-to-point channel) and tends to grow into an unmaintainable rule tangle; splitting into several brokers loses the single maintenance point, while a hierarchy of local brokers under a central one decouples whole subsystems like network subnets.

hooks.clause: an instance's own harness as a local broker under the core's central one: decouple subsystems, not just scripts

tools.title: Transformation complements routing; metadata management
tools.definition: Routers hide where receivers are but not what format they need, so translators complete the decoupling; the chapter also treats metadata (data definitions) as a parallel concern that adapters can extract into repositories and tools can import and export.

hooks.clause: codebooks are the metadata repository; projections are the translators

tools.title: Envelope Wrapper

transform.reason: No header, encryption, or payload encapsulation transform exists.

observable: Infrastructure fields surround an unchanged application payload.

tools.definition: When the messaging infrastructure requires header fields or formats (encryption, routing data) the applications know nothing about, a wrapper puts the application message inside a compliant envelope at the boundary and an unwrapper removes it at the far side.

hooks.clause: the publication compiler wraps an internal record in the envelope a target requires (PR body, release notes) and strips it on the way back
a receipt envelope (writer, time, version, correlation) around an unchanged payload

tools.title: Wrapping steps and chained envelopes

transform.reason: No nested payload representation or reversible wrapper operation is defined.

observable: Envelope layers are added and removed in the required order.

tools.definition: Wrapping is a fixed sequence (take the raw message, add the required header, possibly transform or encrypt the body, hand to the infrastructure) that reverses on the way out; envelopes nest when a message crosses several infrastructures, like a letter in a courier bag, and each layer must be removed in order.

hooks.clause: a record crossing instance, kit and core boundaries picks up and sheds one envelope per boundary

verified.note: model-knowledge (the site excerpt omits the steps and nesting)

tools.title: Operational complexity
tools.definition: Deploying, monitoring and troubleshooting a distributed solution built from mixed technologies is hard; this motivates the system-management patterns.

place.chapter: Chapter 1: Solving Integration Problems Using Patterns

hooks.clause: status and beacons exist because distributed heterogeneous flows are hard to see

tools.title: Content Enricher

transform.reason: No lookup service, field schema, or payload insertion transform is available.

observable: A request gains fields needed by its next receiver.

tools.definition: When the sender lacks data the receiver needs, a filter uses keys in the message to look up or compute the missing information and appends it; sources are computation, the environment (current time), or another system, including a human entering data.

hooks.clause: a pull-request body enriched with evidence references and version data looked up from records
an order enriched at dispatch with the context a role needs instead of each role looking it up

tools.title: Content Filter

transform.reason: No payload-field deletion or flattening transform is available.

observable: A receiver sees a smaller permitted set of fields.

tools.definition: Removes data items a receiver does not need (or must not see) and can flatten deep, repeating structures into a simple list, so a large message becomes the small one the receiver can process.

hooks.clause: outward lint is a content filter: strip employer material and internals before anything leaves
the clean-room screen on intake is a content filter applied before synthesis

tools.title: Content filter vs message filter; security use

transform.reason: No field-level payload operation is available for the content-removal branch.

observable: Traffic volume and visible fields change under different filters.

tools.definition: A message filter drops whole messages, a content filter drops fields inside a message that passes; removing sensitive fields before a message leaves a trust boundary is a security use the pattern explicitly serves.

hooks.clause: publication needs both: refuse some records entirely, redact fields in the rest

verified.note: model-knowledge (the site excerpt omits the security use and the comparison)

tools.title: Claim Check

transform.reason: No external payload store, handle creation, and retrieval transform is defined.

observable: Small handle messages replace data until a later retrieval.

tools.definition: Data needed only later is stored in a persistent store under a unique component-generated key, stripped from the message, and the key travels instead; a later content enricher uses the key to retrieve the data, keeping messages small and the flow fast.

hooks.clause: receipts cite evidence by path and hash instead of embedding it: the claim check is already the record style
evidence directories are the store; the order record carries the ticket

tools.title: Claim-check key choice and store management

transform.reason: No handle collision model or external-store lifecycle contract is supplied.

observable: Stored payloads remain or expire after handle use.

tools.definition: The key may be a business key, a message id, or a generated handle; the store needs a removal policy (delete on retrieval, expire, or keep for audit) and gains a security side benefit because sensitive data never travels with the message.

hooks.clause: a content hash as the claim key makes the ticket self-verifying; state the retention rule for the store

verified.note: model-knowledge (the site excerpt omits key criteria and cleanup)

tools.title: Normalizer

transform.reason: No format recogniser and field-mapping transforms are defined.

observable: Equivalent incoming records leave in one representation.

tools.definition: Semantically equivalent messages arrive in many formats; a router detects each incoming format and hands the message to the matching translator so all output shares one common format. Detection uses a type header, or failing that the document's root element, path checks, delimited field counts and types, or file names and folders.

hooks.clause: the feedback compiler is a normaliser over heterogeneous feedback sources into one rule format
channel-plural intake (chat exports, images, notes) normalised to one unit record by detected format

tools.title: Canonical Data Model

transform.reason: No canonical schema or bidirectional payload mapping is supplied.

observable: Each unit exchanges one common record representation.

tools.definition: An application-independent common format that every participant translates to and from, so n applications need about 2n translators instead of n(n-1) direct ones; it feels like overkill for few applications and pays off as the count grows.

hooks.clause: the record codebooks are the canonical model; every host and UI translates to them, never to each other
IR compatibility between core and forks is a canonical-model question

tools.title: Canonical model costs: double translation, model design, body-only scope, evolution

transform.reason: No schema evolution, conversion cost, or compatibility model is supplied.

observable: Two boundary conversions add work to unit exchanges.

tools.definition: Every message is translated twice; designing a model everyone accepts is hard and political; the model should cover the message body and leave infrastructure headers alone; and it must evolve, which is what a format indicator on each message makes possible.

hooks.clause: version the codebook and carry the version in each record; do not let one UI's needs leak into the canonical shape

verified.note: model-knowledge (the site excerpt gives only the translator count argument)

tools.title: Loan broker scenario and participants
tools.definition: A running example for composing patterns: a customer gives a broker an identifier, amount and term; the broker fetches a credit score from a bureau, asks several banks for quotes, and returns the best; the broker is the system being designed, the bureau and banks are outside services.

hooks.clause: the loan broker is the canonical shape of a fan-out brief: enrich, ask many, pick

tools.title: Design choice: obtaining the credit score with a content enricher

transform.reason: No external-data lookup schema or payload append transform is available.

observable: Provider requests include a complete set of required facts.

tools.definition: The broker enriches the customer request with bureau data before asking banks, so banks receive a complete request and the broker owns the dependency on the bureau.

hooks.clause: enrich the order with context once at dispatch rather than making every worker fetch it

tools.title: Information Portal

transform.reason: No view composition or multi-source query transform is defined.

observable: A combined view of state reported by twenty units.

tools.definition: Integration whose goal is one display that aggregates data from several systems for a user, without the systems otherwise cooperating.

place.chapter: Chapter 1: Solving Integration Problems Using Patterns

hooks.clause: the board is an information portal over control log, receipts and status

tools.title: Design choice: fixed bank list vs criteria-based distribution vs auction

transform.reason: No eligibility predicate, provider registry, or comparison objective is supplied.

observable: Provider participation changes with the selection design.

tools.definition: Which banks to ask can be a fixed list, a list computed from the request by a second enricher (distribution), or left open by publishing the request so interested banks subscribe (auction); each shifts knowledge of recipients from broker to rules to the banks themselves.

hooks.clause: a fixed worker roster, a computed roster, or an open call: each needs a different completeness rule

tools.title: Design choice: sequential synchronous vs parallel asynchronous requests

transform.reason: No request lifecycle and multi-reply completion model is defined.

observable: Concurrent unit requests reduce waiting but reorder replies.

tools.definition: Asking banks one at a time is simple but slow and blocks; asking all at once is fast but replies arrive in any order and must be matched and buffered.

hooks.clause: parallel fan-out saves wall-clock time only if the aggregation and correlation are designed; otherwise serial is honest

tools.title: Design choice: one shared reply channel with correlation vs one reply channel per bank

transform.reason: No correlation-key or reply-channel allocation contract is supplied.

observable: Channel count trades against reply matching work.

tools.definition: A single reply channel needs correlation identifiers to tell replies apart but scales to any number of banks; a channel per bank needs no correlation but multiplies channels and ties the broker to the bank set.

hooks.clause: one handback stream keyed by dispatch id versus a file per worker; the stream scales, the files need no correlation

tools.title: Design choice: pool of broker instances with a dispatcher vs a single event-driven instance

transform.reason: No instance state ownership and processor scheduling model is supplied.

observable: Concurrent requests distribute across coordinator instances.

tools.definition: Concurrency can come from many broker instances fed by a message dispatcher or from one event-driven instance that keeps per-request state; the first scales CPU, the second keeps state simple.

hooks.clause: lanes with several workers versus one resident holding all request state: the dispatcher decision

tools.title: Patterns composed in the loan broker
tools.definition: Content enricher (twice), scatter-gather via recipient list or publish-subscribe, aggregator, translator or normaliser for bank formats, correlation identifier, message filter or selective consumer, point-to-point channels, and a message dispatcher: one design walks a dozen patterns.

tools.title: Variant A: synchronous web services (Java/Axis)
tools.definition: Blocking SOAP calls to a credit agency and five banks exposed as separate services; an enricher adds credit data, a recipient list picks eligible banks, banks are called in turn with their own request and reply so no correlation is needed, and the aggregator keeps the lowest rate; no normaliser because replies share one format.

hooks.clause: serial worker calls: simplest, no correlation, latency adds up per worker

tools.title: Lesson: latency accumulates and degrades under load in synchronous composition
tools.definition: Sequential single-threaded calls avoid concurrency bugs, but the customer waits for the sum of all bank latencies and response time rises steeply as concurrent clients increase (the chapter reports roughly doubling from one to four clients).

related.title: Messaging challenges: complex programming model, sequence issues, synchronous scenarios, performance, limited platform support, vendor lock-in

hooks.clause: an operator running roles serially pays the sum of their times; measure before promising parallel speedups

tools.title: Variant B: asynchronous queues (C#/MSMQ)
tools.definition: Gateways keep messaging out of business logic; requesters supply a return address; a recipient list and aggregator form a scatter-gather; a process-manager dictionary tracks each concurrent request; the broker is event-driven on one thread while extra credit-bureau instances compete on the request queue.

observable: Replies retain identity even if intermediaries replace message identifiers.

tools.definition: Replies are correlated by an application-chosen token carried in the request and echoed back (the completion-token idiom) rather than by the infrastructure's message id, so intermediaries that re-send the message do not break correlation.

hooks.clause: generate the dispatch id yourself and require the handback to echo it; never rely on a host's own call identifiers

transform.reason: No transaction begin, commit, rollback, or atomic multi-operation model is defined.

observable: Sends and consumes become visible together only after commit.

tools.definition: The client's messaging session is transactional so it controls the boundaries: a sent message appears on the channel only at commit and a received message leaves the channel only at commit; explicit and implicit transactions can mix across parties, at a cost in widely distributed systems (cloud queues often substitute a visibility timeout).

tools.title: Polling Consumer

observable: A ready receiver takes queued work only on its polling schedule.

tools.definition: The application asks the channel for a message when it is ready, processes it, then asks again; blocking and non-blocking receives differ when polling outpaces arrivals.

hooks.clause: the operator checking status is a polling consumer; the cost is wasted polls, the benefit is control of pace

tools.title: Event-Driven Consumer

observable: A waiting receiver is notified when a message arrives without polling empty queues.

tools.definition: The messaging system invokes the application's callback as each message arrives, so the receiver needs no active thread while idle and never polls an empty channel.

place.part: Pattern catalog: endpoints and system management (chapters 10–11)

hooks.clause: hooks are event-driven consumers of tool-call events; their rate is set by the host, not by them

transform.reason: No common arrival-rate and receiver-capacity model is supplied for the comparison.

observable: Pickup delay and idle work vary between two receive schedules.

tools.definition: Polling gives the consumer the strongest throttle (it decides when to take work) at the price of empty polls and latency; event-driven consumption wastes nothing and reacts at once but accepts whatever rate the channel delivers, bounded only by how many consumers exist.

hooks.clause: attention is a throttle: a polling operator paces work, an event-driven resident reacts; name which the workflow assumes

observable: One dispatcher gives each queued message to one available performer.

tools.definition: One consumer takes each message from the channel and hands it to one of several performers, which may be pooled, concurrent in their own threads, or specialised so that each message reaches a suitable performer; coordination lives in the dispatcher rather than in the channel.

observable: Coordination moves from channel delivery to a dispatching unit.

tools.definition: Competing consumers let the channel distribute work with no coordinator but only on point-to-point channels and with no say over which consumer gets what; a dispatcher works on any channel, including publish-subscribe, and can route to specialised performers, at the cost of being a component to maintain; the structure echoes the Reactor idiom.

tools.title: Selective Consumer

observable: A consumer receives only messages whose numeric selector matches its threshold.

tools.definition: A consumer declares criteria over selection values the producer set and receives only matching messages, so one channel behaves like several datatype channels; on a point-to-point channel, messages matching no consumer's criteria are never consumed and clutter the channel until they expire.

tools.title: Idempotent Receiver

observable: Repeated identifiers within the retention window do not trigger a second delivery.

tools.definition: A receiver designed so that getting the same message more than once has the same effect as once, because at-least-once delivery and resends make duplicates inevitable; achieved by explicit de-duplication or by message semantics that are naturally repeatable.

transform.reason: No receiver state-update vocabulary exists to compare semantic and explicit duplicate safety.

observable: Repeated requests may need memory or may leave unit state unchanged.

tools.definition: Tracking seen message ids needs a store and a rule for how long to remember (too short admits late duplicates, too long grows without bound); designing operations as absolute assignments (set the balance) rather than relative changes (add to the balance) removes the need to track at all.

observable: The same unit operation is reachable directly or through queued input.

tools.definition: An endpoint that receives a message, invokes an ordinary service with its contents, and optionally sends the result back as a reply, so the same service is reachable both through messaging and by direct synchronous call without knowing which.

tools.definition: A fixed recipient list with two outputs that forwards each message unchanged to its main channel and copies it to a secondary channel for inspection, so analysis can be added to any point-to-point channel without changing its behaviour.

tools.title: Asynchronous Request-Response (conversation)

transform.reason: Timeout alone cannot express reply correlation and requester conversation state.

observable: A late response leaves the requesting unit unsure of provider completion.

tools.definition: The requestor sends a request and awaits a separate response matched by a correlation identifier; the provider keeps no conversation state, so the requestor must time out on lost or late responses while remaining unsure of the provider's state.

place.part: Conversation Patterns (book website, work in progress, last updated January 2017; not part of the 2003 book)

hooks.clause: after a dispatch times out the worker's state is unknown; the brief must say what the requestor then assumes

tools.title: Request-Response with Retry (conversation)

transform.reason: No shared request identity, duplicate-safe effect, and circuit-breaker state machine is defined.

observable: A request retries with increasing delay before an explicit give-up outcome.

tools.definition: After a timeout, resend the request with the same correlation identifier so the provider can detect the duplicate; both sides must be idempotent; cap the retries, back off exponentially, add a circuit breaker, and then report an error.

place.part: Conversation Patterns (book website, work in progress, last updated January 2017; not part of the 2003 book)

hooks.clause: re-dispatch a silent worker under the same dispatch id; cap retries from the budget and record the give-up as an error
retry caps and back-off are time-budget policy, stated once

tools.title: Polling (conversation)

observable: A completed result remains queued until the requestor next polls for it.

tools.definition: When a requestor cannot receive unsolicited messages (firewalls, program design) it repeatedly asks until the provider's stored result is ready; shorter intervals cut delay but load the provider, longer ones save load but delay pickup.

place.part: Conversation Patterns (book website, work in progress, last updated January 2017; not part of the 2003 book)

hooks.clause: the operator's status checks are polling; the interval is attention cost against pickup delay

tools.title: Subscribe-Notify (conversation)

observable: An active recipient receives updates until its subscription lease expires without renewal.

tools.definition: For data too large, time-sensitive or endless for one message, the consumer subscribes once and the provider sends notifications as events occur; the subscription ends on unsubscribe, lease expiry without renewal, connection close, provider notice or timeout.

place.part: Conversation Patterns (book website, work in progress, last updated January 2017; not part of the 2003 book)

hooks.clause: board and resident subscriptions need a stated end condition, including lease expiry
a registered target's subscription to releases should lapse without renewal

tools.title: Quick Acknowledgment (conversation)

transform.reason: No acceptance-validation state and separate receipt/result message generator is available.

observable: A requester distinguishes accepted work from a completed outcome.

tools.definition: For a long-running operation the provider replies promptly after receiving and validating the request to confirm that processing began (or to report an early error), usually with a correlation identifier for follow-up; the result arrives later by a result message or by polling.

place.part: Conversation Patterns (book website, work in progress, last updated January 2017; not part of the 2003 book)

hooks.clause: a receipt is a quick acknowledgment: accepted and valid, result to follow; keep receipt and verdict as distinct record kinds
a role should acknowledge an order before working it so the operator can stop waiting

tools.title: Proxy (conversation)

observable: An initiator sends to one intermediary channel that forwards to the partner.

tools.definition: An intermediary forwards messages between an initiator and a partner that cannot be reached directly (segmentation, access restriction, screening, anonymity), usually one-way, shielding the partner from inbound requests.

place.part: Conversation Patterns (book website, work in progress, last updated January 2017; not part of the 2003 book)

hooks.clause: the harness proxies every write so hosts never touch gate inputs directly

tools.title: Relay (conversation)

observable: The intermediary queues incoming messages until an outbound polling recipient retrieves them.

tools.definition: When participants can only make outbound requests, both send to a relay that stores messages until the recipient polls and retrieves them, making two-way conversation possible through one-way reach.

place.part: Conversation Patterns (book website, work in progress, last updated January 2017; not part of the 2003 book)

hooks.clause: the resident's loopback is a relay: both sides append to the log and the other side polls it
relayed records need expiry or they accumulate for a recipient that never polls

tools.title: Load Balancer (conversation)

observable: An intermediary assigns each message to one provider with available capacity.

tools.definition: Identical providers that do not know each other share incoming messages through an intermediary that distributes them, sometimes keeping related messages together using information the providers share.

place.part: Conversation Patterns (book website, work in progress, last updated January 2017; not part of the 2003 book)

hooks.clause: lanes balancing orders across worker sessions while keeping one order's records with one worker

tools.title: Scatter-Gather (conversation)

transform.reason: No per-partner conversation state and combined-result transform is available.

observable: One coordinator tracks several provider exchanges for one requesting unit.

tools.definition: A requestor gets answers from many providers without talking to each: the intermediary relays the request and aggregates replies; unlike the messaging version it holds conversation state with both the requestor and each provider across request-response exchanges.

place.part: Conversation Patterns (book website, work in progress, last updated January 2017; not part of the 2003 book)

hooks.clause: a fan-out coordinator keeps a conversation with each worker (acknowledge, retry, result), not just a reply slot

tools.title: Heartbeat (conversation)

transform.reason: No periodic heartbeat generator and missed-beat observer transition is defined.

observable: An observer marks units silent after several expected beats are absent.

tools.definition: Each component periodically sends a heartbeat and an observer alerts or acts when the beats stop, avoiding central pinging (which adds load, a single point of failure and a registration requirement); interval and missed-beat threshold are left to the implementer.

place.part: Conversation Patterns (book website, work in progress, last updated January 2017; not part of the 2003 book)

related.title: Heartbeat vs test message (alive vs correct)

hooks.clause: beacon age is the missed-beat threshold; state it per beacon kind and alarm on it

transform.reason: The toy lacks check results, message splitting, and result merging.

observable: Validated requests and completed item groups.

tools.definition: A publish-subscribe fork runs credit and inventory checks in parallel, an aggregator joins the results, a content-based router separates valid from invalid orders (the latter onto an invalid-message channel), and a splitter plus router plus aggregator form a composed processor over the order items.

hooks.clause: an order's verification and review as parallel checks aggregated into one verdict

tools.title: Stranded resources; explicit vs implicit termination; who may end and who keeps alive a conversation
tools.definition: Some conversations never end naturally and providers hold storage, connections or money for consumers that may vanish silently, so resources strand and exhaust; the introduction asks whether termination is explicit or implicit, who may end the conversation, who keeps it alive, and whether the end is announced.

hooks.clause: writer reservations, subagent slots and budgets are held resources; each needs an answer to who ends it and how

tools.title: Incremental State Build-up (conversation)

transform.reason: No partial-payload accumulation and operation-ready predicate is defined.

observable: A unit begins its operation only after enough input pieces arrive.

tools.definition: When a requestor lacks all the data for an operation at once (or it exceeds message limits), it sends the pieces over several messages and the provider accumulates them until it can run the operation.

hooks.clause: evidence accumulates in the order's directory until the gate can run; the gate is the operation

tools.title: Lease (conversation)

transform.reason: Resource grant, renewal, and release states are absent from the closed transforms.

observable: An unrenewed holding becomes available again after its lease ends.

tools.definition: Grant a resource for a limited time; the holder must renew before expiry and unrenewed resources are freed, so a holder that dies releases its resources by silence; shorter leases reclaim faster at the cost of renewal traffic, longer leases tie resources up.

place.part: Conversation Patterns (book website, work in progress, last updated January 2017; not part of the 2003 book)

hooks.clause: make the per-worktree writer reservation a lease with renewal and expiry so a crashed session cannot hold the writer forever
lease length is the trade between reclaiming a dead session fast and renewal noise

tools.title: Renewal Reminder (conversation)

transform.reason: No held-resource lifecycle or holder response transition is defined.

observable: A provider releases a holding when its owner does not confirm continued use.

tools.definition: The provider periodically pings holders and releases any resource whose holder declines or does not answer, putting the liveness check on the provider's side instead of the holder's.

place.part: Conversation Patterns (book website, work in progress, last updated January 2017; not part of the 2003 book)

hooks.clause: the harness pings the writer holder and releases the reservation on silence, the inverse of the holder renewing

tools.title: Consistency without transactions: optimistic vs pessimistic; most likely failure first, hardest-to-revert last

transform.reason: No failure probabilities, reversibility model, and transactional step sequence is supplied.

observable: Risky early steps and delayed irreversible steps change recovery exposure.

tools.definition: Distributed participants cannot rely on atomic transactions, so they reach consistency by conversation under uncertainty about each other's state; strategies range from ignoring errors through retry and compensation to tentative operations and coordinated agreement, and two ordering rules reduce exposure: do the step most likely to fail first and the hardest-to-undo step last.

place.part: Conversation Patterns (book website, work in progress, last updated January 2017; not part of the 2003 book)

related.title: WS-Coordination and WS-Transaction: atomic transaction vs business activity

hooks.clause: order gate steps cheapest-likely-fail first and publication last; release-close after final review is the hardest-to-revert-last rule
publishing is the hardest step to undo, so it is the last step

tools.title: Ignore Error (conversation)

observable: A failed delivery receives no retry and the sender continues to later messages.

tools.definition: The requestor disregards a failed call and carries on, accepting occasional loss in exchange for simplicity and throughput; the introduction notes this is more often adequate than engineers expect.

place.part: Conversation Patterns (book website, work in progress, last updated January 2017; not part of the 2003 book)

hooks.clause: a lost beacon or a failed optional projection refresh can be ignored by policy, if the policy is written down

tools.title: Compensating Action (conversation)

transform.reason: No forward and compensating operation pairs or recovery state machine are defined.

observable: Completed unit effects are undone in reverse sequence where possible.

tools.definition: Act optimistically across independent services, then on a mid-way failure undo completed steps with compensating actions (in reverse order in a saga); compensation may fail, may only approximate the prior state, or be impossible, so schedule the hardest-to-revert action last.

place.part: Conversation Patterns (book website, work in progress, last updated January 2017; not part of the 2003 book)

related.title: WS-Coordination and WS-Transaction: atomic transaction vs business activity

hooks.clause: repair (resume: fix) and release rollback are compensations; list each lifecycle step's compensating action and which cannot be undone

tools.title: Tentative Operation (conversation)

transform.reason: No provisional resource state and confirm, cancel, and expiry transitions are available.

observable: A tentative effect becomes final only after later confirmation.

tools.definition: Make a provisional hold first (try), then confirm or cancel once the other steps succeed; if the requestor never confirms, the provider releases the hold when its timeout expires, so hard-to-reverse actions are never taken speculatively.

place.part: Conversation Patterns (book website, work in progress, last updated January 2017; not part of the 2003 book)

hooks.clause: staging a version before final review is a tentative operation; give staged versions an expiry so abandoned ones release themselves
a draft release that auto-cancels if not confirmed

tools.title: Coordinated Agreement (conversation)

transform.reason: No agreement protocol, vote states, or atomic confirm/cancel operation is defined.

observable: All participating units either accept one outcome or decline it.

tools.definition: When independent participants must all act or none, a coordinator gathers each one's response, finds an outcome everyone can accept if any exists, and distributes it; the all-confirm-or-all-cancel strategy resembles two-phase commit.

place.part: Conversation Patterns (book website, work in progress, last updated January 2017; not part of the 2003 book)

hooks.clause: final review is the coordinator gathering verification and review verdicts into one accepted outcome
sealed adjudication of opinion cohorts is a coordinated agreement over independent judgments

observable: An origin unit can inspect progress through several stages.

tools.definition: Progress is tracked by tapping the flow into a store; central storage enables a claim check; promoting the store to a process manager lets it decide next steps; the web interface reads status from a shared database; a smart proxy adds reply-address support to legacy services.

hooks.clause: status is a projection over a tapped record store, not a separate write path

hooks.clause: a fixed icon vocabulary for sketching control-plane flows in planning documents

observable: Consistency of data available when a unit processes a request.

hooks.clause: carry needed state inside a record versus propagating it through a side channel; prefer self-contained records

tools.definition: Bulk, periodic supplier catalogs arrive as files and are processed whole by translators: a reminder that file transfer is the right style for large infrequent batches.

hooks.clause: kit exports are bulk periodic transfers, not message streams

observable: Announcement recipients vary with registered interests.

tools.definition: A composite of Recipient List and Dynamic Router: recipients register their subscription preferences on a control channel and the list is computed from them per announcement.

hooks.clause: publication fan-out to registered targets computed from their declared interests

observable: Detected bad replies and measured response delays.

tools.title: Six pattern categories (construction, routing, transformation, endpoints, channels, system management) with root patterns as entry points
tools.definition: The language is organised into six categories, each entered through one root pattern from chapter 3; chapter 1 presents the categories as the book's organising scheme.

place.chapter: Chapter 1: Solving Integration Problems Using Patterns

tools.title: Eight integration criteria
tools.definition: Styles are compared on: whether applications need to collaborate at all; application coupling (assumptions made); integration simplicity (how intrusive the change is); integration technology required; data format and its evolvability; data timeliness; whether data or functionality is shared; and asynchronicity.

hooks.clause: a criteria list for comparing candidate designs in a planning pass

tools.title: Styles ordered by increasing sophistication; mix styles per connection

transform.reason: No scored style-selection rule or connection-reconfiguration transform is defined.

observable: Different unit connections use different exchange styles.

tools.definition: The four styles are presented in order, each addressing shortcomings of the previous; no style is always right, one application may use different styles on different connections, and products combine them internally.

hooks.clause: an instance can mix file-style kit updates with message-style control records; pick per connection

tools.title: Why messaging gets the most attention
tools.definition: Messaging is treated at length because the authors judge it the best fit most often, the least understood of the four, and the foundation of most integration products.

tools.title: Messaging as asynchronous, decoupled communication
tools.definition: Applications hand data to a messaging system that transfers it on their behalf, so sender and receiver need not run at the same time and each focuses on what to share rather than how.

hooks.clause: writers append; readers project later; the log is the messaging system

tools.title: Channels are created, not given
tools.definition: A new messaging system has no channels; the designers create the set of named virtual pipes their applications need, which makes channel design a first-class decision.

hooks.clause: which record kinds get their own log or index is a channel-design decision

tools.title: Pattern form (name, icon, context, problem, forces, solution, sketch, results, next patterns, sidebars, examples)

transform.reason: No document-composition transform or pattern-entry schema is defined.

observable: Completeness of a candidate pattern description.

tools.definition: Each pattern follows one written template: the context it arises in, a one-sentence problem question, the forces that make it hard, the solution with a sketch, the resulting context, pointers to the patterns that come next, and implementation sidebars and examples.

hooks.clause: a fixed template (problem question, forces, solution, resulting context, next) for idea-ledger entries and pattern-library rows

tools.title: Message as atomic packet; delivery retried until it succeeds
tools.definition: Data is split into packets, each wrapped as a message and sent on a channel; the messaging system keeps retrying delivery until it succeeds, which is the basis of reliability.

hooks.clause: a receipt is an atomic packet; its delivery to projections should be retried, never assumed

tools.title: Five-step transmission: create, send, deliver, receive, process
tools.definition: The sender creates and sends a message; the messaging system delivers it; the receiver receives and then processes it; the split clarifies where reliability and failure handling live.

hooks.clause: a hook event is delivered when logged, received when read, processed when acted on; receipts should say which

verified.note: model-knowledge (the site intro omits the step list)

tools.title: Multi-step delivery, routing, transformation, endpoints
tools.definition: Between sender and receiver a message may be validated, transformed (translator), directed through a channel topology (router) and chained through steps (pipes and filters), with endpoint code attaching each application.

tools.title: File Transfer

transform.reason: No file export, import, and translation operations are defined.

observable: Periodic transfer of batches between unit groups.

tools.definition: Each application exports files of shared data on a business-suited schedule and others import them; integrators transform the files because producer output rarely matches consumer needs, and format choice is the central decision.

hooks.clause: kit exports and starter refreshes are file-transfer integration between core and instances

tools.title: File Transfer trade-offs

transform.reason: No data-staleness, concurrent-update, and file-format comparison model is defined.

observable: Data age and coordination demands of batch exchange.

tools.definition: Strong decoupling in technology and time with no shared middleware, but data goes stale between transfers, formats and file naming need agreement, concurrent updates are not coordinated, and heavy file processing is required.

hooks.clause: an exported kit is stale until the next export; name and version files so instances can tell

verified.note: eip-site:FileTransferIntegration.html (format, processing, timing); model-knowledge (staleness, update coordination)

tools.title: Shared Database

transform.reason: No database schema, transaction, or concurrent-write transform is available.

observable: Twenty units read and write a shared state.

tools.definition: All applications store shared data in one database so it is always consistent and timely, with transactions handling concurrent updates and errors surfacing quickly.

hooks.clause: the shared-database shape is the anti-shape of the append-only log; status is read from projections instead

tools.title: Shared Database trade-offs

transform.reason: No schema ownership, locking, or database capacity model is specified.

observable: Units wait when shared writes contend.

tools.definition: One schema for everyone is very hard to design and politically contested; packaged applications cannot adopt it; and a single database becomes a performance and locking bottleneck tied to one vendor.

verified.note: eip-site:SharedDataBaseIntegration.html (schema, politics); model-knowledge (performance, lock contention, vendor lock-in)

tools.title: Remote Procedure Invocation

transform.reason: No procedure vocabulary, input schema, or remote result contract is defined.

observable: One unit waits for an operation on another unit.

tools.definition: Each application is an encapsulated component owning its data and exposing procedures; others ask it for data or ask it to change data, so internals can change behind the interface.

hooks.clause: a synchronous subagent call is RPI-shaped: encapsulated, but coupled in time and availability

tools.title: Remote Procedure Invocation trade-offs

transform.reason: No call-dependency graph or partial-failure semantics are defined.

observable: Failed and delayed calls block dependent units.

tools.definition: Encapsulation beats a shared data structure, yet the calls weave a growing web of dependencies, required call sequences hinder independent change, both parties must be up at once, and local-call syntax hides remote failure modes.

related.title: The illusion of local calls (RPC/RMI critique)

tools.title: Messaging (integration style)

transform.reason: The architecture requires a channel topology and payload contracts, not one numeric policy.

observable: Twenty units exchange queued messages through middleware.

tools.definition: Applications exchange small packets of data through a messaging system that delivers them frequently, immediately, reliably and asynchronously, in formats the parties choose.

hooks.clause: DotLn's record flow is the messaging style: small self-contained records, delivered reliably and asynchronously

tools.title: Implementing frameworks (Spring Integration, Apache Camel, Mule, Red Hat Fuse, Guaraná DSL)
tools.definition: Open-source integration frameworks adopted the book's pattern names and icons as their component vocabulary, which is why the names are a lingua franca for messaging toolkits.

tools.title: Messaging benefits: asynchrony, in-transit decoupling, flexible topologies, separation of concerns, better design
tools.definition: Parties need not be up together; messages can be transformed in transit unseen by either side; a message can be broadcast or routed; integration code is developed apart from the applications; and thinking asynchronously pushes toward cohesive, loosely attached components.

hooks.clause: asynchrony is what lets the operator dispatch and walk away; waits are a design choice, not a given

tools.title: Messaging challenges: complex programming model, sequence issues, synchronous scenarios, performance, limited platform support, vendor lock-in

transform.reason: No scenario defines the compared execution model, ordering needs, or cost function.

observable: Delay and ordering errors across asynchronous unit exchanges.

tools.definition: Event-driven code is harder to write and debug than a call stack; messages can arrive out of order; some interactions genuinely need an immediate answer; store-and-forward costs latency; not every platform has a client; and products differ, which locks you in.

hooks.clause: out-of-order worker returns and genuinely synchronous questions are the two costs to design for in fan-out

verified.note: eip-site:Introduction.html (complex programming, sequencing named); model-knowledge (remaining items)

tools.title: Message Channel
tools.definition: A named virtual pipe between applications: one side writes, the other reads, and because channels are dedicated to kinds of information each party picks a channel by content without knowing the other.

hooks.clause: the control log and each receipt stream are channels; name them by information kind

tools.title: Message
tools.definition: The unit the messaging system transmits: a header of metadata the system uses (origin, destination, identifiers) and a body carrying the application data, normally passed through unchanged.

hooks.clause: separate a record's envelope (who, when, correlation, version) from its payload

tools.title: Pipes and Filters

transform.reason: No filter operation schema or pipeline topology mutation is defined.

observable: A message passes through reusable processing stages.

tools.definition: Break a processing task into independent filters joined by channels (pipes); because every filter reads from one pipe and writes to another through a shared interface, filters can be added, removed, reordered or reused without changing each other.

hooks.clause: the hook chain and gate steps are a pipeline; keep each step single-purpose and recomposable
feedback compiler stages as filters over a stream of feedback records

tools.title: Pipeline trade-offs: parallel filter instances vs channel overhead and harder tracing

transform.reason: No stage service-time and per-hop overhead model is supplied.

observable: Throughput and delay as unit processing stages increase.

tools.definition: Independent filters can run in parallel copies to raise throughput and can be tested alone, but every extra pipe costs latency and serialisation, and following one message through many steps is hard without history or tracing support.

hooks.clause: tracing a record across many steps needs a carried history, not just per-step receipts

verified.note: model-knowledge (the site excerpt names independence and flexibility only)

tools.title: Stateless vs stateful filters
tools.definition: Most filters hold no state between messages and can be replicated freely; aggregators, resequencers and similar filters keep state across messages, which constrains replication and demands persistence.

hooks.clause: a verdict aggregator over workers is stateful; only stateless steps may fan out freely

verified.note: model-knowledge; eip-site:Aggregator.html and Resequencer.html (both called stateful filters)

tools.title: Message Router

transform.reason: A routing condition and destination map are needed before a faithful policy can be set.

observable: Messages choose among output channels without payload changes.

tools.definition: A filter that consumes from one channel and republishes to one of several output channels according to conditions, changing only the destination, not the content, so routing rules live in one place and messages pass through in order.

hooks.clause: the scheduler and lanes are a router over orders; keep routing rules in one visible place

tools.title: Router trade-offs: central rules vs hidden dependency, inspection cost, and pub-sub plus filters as the alternative

transform.reason: No destination rules or traffic-cost comparison contract is specified.

observable: Copies and routing decisions move between hub and receivers.

tools.definition: A router decouples senders from destinations and centralises change, but it must read message content, adds a hop, and becomes a dependency every flow silently relies on; broadcasting on a publish-subscribe channel with a filter at each receiver pushes the decision to the edges instead.

hooks.clause: central routing in the harness versus each hook filtering what it handles: name which you chose

tools.title: Router taxonomy: fixed, content-based, context-based; stateless vs stateful
tools.definition: Routers are classified by what drives the decision (a fixed rule, the message content, or external context such as a test result or control command) and by whether earlier messages influence the decision.

hooks.clause: a context-based router is what operator override and detour toggles turn on

tools.title: Application sprawl
tools.definition: Enterprises run hundreds or thousands of custom, packaged and legacy applications on many platforms; no single application, not even a large ERP suite, covers the business, so integration is unavoidable.

place.chapter: Chapter 1: Solving Integration Problems Using Patterns

tools.title: Message Translator

transform.reason: No payload mapping schema or data-conversion transform exists.

observable: Unit messages change representation while retaining meaning.

tools.definition: A filter placed between parties that converts one data format into another so applications with proprietary models (or partners using industry standards) can exchange messages; the messaging analogue of the object-oriented Adapter.

hooks.clause: the publication compiler is a translator from internal records to outward surfaces
projections are translators from log records to indexes and status

tools.title: Levels of transformation: transport, data representation, data types, data structure
tools.definition: Translation is layered: the transport protocol, the wire representation (encoding, character set, syntax), field types and value domains, and the application-level structure and semantics; translators are chained so each handles one layer.

hooks.clause: feedback normalisation has the same layers: file syntax, field types, then meaning
