tools.title: Message Endpoint
tools.definition: The code that attaches an application to a channel: a sending endpoint turns data or requests into messages, a receiving endpoint extracts message contents for the application, shielding the rest of the application from the messaging API.

hooks.clause: console, board and resident are endpoints on the record streams
the kit's scripts are the endpoint code an instance uses to read and write records

tools.title: Channel design themes: one-to-one vs one-to-many, typed channels, error channels, crash-proofing, non-messaging clients, backbone
tools.definition: Channel decisions group into themes: whether a message has one consumer or many, whether channels are typed, where bad or undeliverable messages go, how channels survive crashes, how non-messaging applications attach, and whether a bus forms the backbone.

hooks.clause: a checklist for each record stream: consumers, type, error destination, durability, external attach

tools.title: Point-to-Point Channel

observable: Each queued message is removed by exactly one competing receiver.

tools.definition: A channel on which each message is consumed by exactly one receiver even when several listen; competing receivers need no coordination because the channel guarantees single consumption, while different messages can still be processed concurrently.

hooks.clause: one writer per worktree is a point-to-point guarantee: an order is consumed by exactly one holder

tools.title: Publish-Subscribe Channel

observable: Every active subscriber receives one copy of each publication.

tools.definition: A channel that delivers a copy of each published event to every subscriber, each copy consumed once; because listening does not disturb traffic, a logging subscriber can observe everything without instrumenting applications.

hooks.clause: beacons and the resident's loopback are publish-subscribe: the board listens without disturbing the flow
an audit listener on the log is the free eavesdropper this pattern promises

tools.title: Datatype Channel

observable: Messages route to the channel matching their numbered data type.

tools.definition: One channel per kind of data so every message on a channel has the same type; the sender picks the channel and the receiver infers the type from where the message arrived, instead of inspecting it.

hooks.clause: separate streams per record kind (control events, receipts, beacons) rather than one mixed log with type sniffing

tools.title: Typed channels vs format indicator vs selective consumer; channel proliferation

transform.reason: No concrete type tags, selector predicates, or channel cost function is specified.

observable: Receiver inspection and channel counts vary with type placement.

tools.definition: Type can be conveyed by the channel, by a marker inside the message, or by a consumer that filters; typed channels are simplest for receivers but multiply channels, while markers keep one channel at the cost of inspection.

verified.note: model-knowledge (the site excerpt lists the alternatives only as related patterns)

tools.title: Invalid Message Channel

observable: A receiver diverts messages it cannot parse to a separate error queue.

tools.definition: A receiver that cannot make sense of a message moves it to a dedicated channel the administrators define, where an error handler can diagnose it; normal traffic never uses the channel, so what accumulates there is a signal.

hooks.clause: a refused or malformed record should land on a visible invalid-record stream, not vanish into a hook's stderr

tools.title: Invalid message vs failed processing; invalid vs dead letter
tools.definition: A message is invalid when the receiver cannot interpret it, not when a well-formed request fails for business reasons (that is a reply, not an invalid message); and it is the receiver that declares invalidity, whereas the messaging system itself parks undeliverable messages on the dead letter channel.

hooks.clause: a verifier's fail verdict is a reply, not an invalid record; keep the two error paths distinct

verified.note: model-knowledge (neither site excerpt draws the distinction)

tools.title: Best-of-breed overlap
tools.definition: Choosing the best application per function leaves overlapping functions and duplicated data across systems that must then be reconciled.

place.chapter: Chapter 1: Solving Integration Problems Using Patterns

tools.title: Dead Letter Channel

observable: Failed or expired deliveries move to a dedicated holding channel.

tools.definition: When the messaging system itself cannot or should not deliver a message (typically expired, addressed to a missing channel, or with no consumer) it moves it to a dead letter channel, usually local to the machine where delivery failed so the move is certain and the failure point recorded.

hooks.clause: a publication that cannot reach its target needs a dead-letter record, locally written, naming where it failed
updates to a registered target that is gone should dead-letter, not retry forever

verified.note: eip-site:DeadLetterChannel.html (problem, who moves it, local placement); model-knowledge (reason list)

tools.title: Guaranteed Delivery

transform.reason: No durable storage, crash, and acknowledgment transition contract is available.

observable: Messages survive unit failures until a recipient confirms receipt.

tools.definition: Store-and-forward persistence: every machine in the path saves the message to local storage before the send counts as done, and a copy is deleted only once the next store has saved it and the receiver acknowledged, so a crash loses nothing.

hooks.clause: append to the control log before acknowledging; a receipt is the acknowledgment, never the only copy

tools.title: Guaranteed Delivery costs and when to skip it

transform.reason: No durable-storage cost or message-value lifetime model is defined.

observable: Recovery benefit and storage work differ across traffic classes.

tools.definition: Persistence costs throughput and disk, and buys nothing for data that is stale by the time it is replayed or for management and test traffic, so guarantee only the messages whose loss matters.

hooks.clause: beacons and heartbeats need not be durable; control decisions and receipts must be

verified.note: model-knowledge (the site excerpt cuts off before costs)

tools.title: Channel Adapter

transform.reason: No application interface or request-to-message mapping is defined.

observable: An otherwise isolated unit exchanges application requests.

tools.definition: A messaging client that attaches an application not built for messaging: it reads the application's API or data to publish messages and turns received messages into application actions, attaching at whichever architectural layer exposes what is needed.

hooks.clause: registered targets are attached through adapters at their edge, not changed inside
UI hosts attach to the record streams through adapter code

tools.title: Adapter attachment layers: user interface, business logic, database; metadata adapters
tools.definition: An adapter may drive the application's screens, call its business API, or read and write its database, each trading intrusiveness against fidelity; a metadata adapter additionally extracts the application's data definitions to configure translators. The adapter emits the application's own format, so a translator is still needed.

hooks.clause: attach to a target at the least intrusive layer that yields the needed record, then translate

verified.note: model-knowledge (the site excerpt says only that layers vary)

tools.title: Messaging Bridge

transform.reason: Cross-system transport and payload conversion contracts are missing.

observable: Messages cross between two unit channel domains.

tools.definition: A set of paired channel adapters that replicates selected channels between two messaging systems, converting formats on the way, so applications join one system yet see messages from the other.

hooks.clause: an instance's record streams and the core's are two messaging systems; bridge selected streams rather than merging logs

tools.title: Message Bus

transform.reason: No common data model, command vocabulary, or adapter contracts are supplied.

observable: Units attach to shared infrastructure through independent endpoints.

tools.definition: Middleware structured so that systems can be added or removed without affecting the others; it combines a common data model and command set, a common communication infrastructure (often routers or publish-subscribe), and an adapter per system.

hooks.clause: the harness is a bus: shared record model, shared log, adapter per host (Claude, Codex, Copilot)

tools.title: Construction decisions: intent, response, large data, slow messages, format change
tools.definition: Building a message raises five decisions: what the message means (command, document or event), how a response comes back (request-reply with return address and correlation), how to carry data too large for one message (sequence), what to do with messages that arrive too late (expiration), and how formats change over time (format indicator).

hooks.clause: a checklist for every record kind: intent, reply path, size, staleness, version

tools.title: Command Message

transform.reason: No concrete procedure vocabulary or command parameter schema is supplied.

observable: A unit receives an explicit request naming the action its sender wants.

tools.definition: A message that tells the receiver which procedure to run and with what parameters, giving the reliability and asynchrony of messaging to what would otherwise be a remote procedure call; normally sent on a point-to-point channel so exactly one receiver executes it.

hooks.clause: a dispatch phrase is a command message; make its parameters explicit and single-consumer
a work order handed to a role is a command, consumed by one holder

tools.title: Document Message
tools.definition: A message whose purpose is to deliver a data structure; the receiver decides what to do with it, content matters more than timing, so guaranteed delivery is usually wanted and expiration usually is not.

hooks.clause: evidence, verification reports and reviews are document messages: the reader decides, the content must not be lost

tools.title: One customer transaction, many systems
tools.definition: A transaction the customer experiences as one step (placing an order) typically crosses five or six systems, so the quality of the integration is the quality the customer sees.

place.chapter: Chapter 1: Solving Integration Problems Using Patterns

hooks.clause: one dispatch phrase crosses many role scripts; the operator experiences the chain as one transaction

tools.title: Event Message
tools.definition: A message that announces that something changed, sent as it happens; timing matters more than content (many events carry nothing but their occurrence), so expiration is useful and the receiver reacts rather than being told what to do.

hooks.clause: control-log entries and beacons are event messages: time-stamped announcements others react to

tools.title: Observer over messaging: push vs pull notification

transform.reason: No state-retrieval payload and notification protocol is specified.

observable: Notifications and follow-up queries use different traffic volumes.

tools.definition: A subject can push the changed data inside the event (fewer round trips, larger messages, every observer gets everything) or push a bare notification that observers answer with a pull request for what they need (smaller events, extra request-reply); the chapter's publish-subscribe example works through both.

hooks.clause: the board can be told only that something changed and pull the projection, instead of receiving whole state in every beacon

tools.title: Intent trichotomy: command vs document vs event

transform.reason: No receiver action vocabulary or intent-dependent payload contract is defined.

observable: The same data prompts different receiver decisions.

tools.definition: The same payload can be sent as an instruction (sender decides the action), as data (receiver decides), or as an announcement (timing dominates); the choice fixes coupling, channel type, durability and expiration defaults.

hooks.clause: classify every record kind by intent; the classification decides durability and consumer rules

tools.title: Request-Reply

transform.reason: No request correlation, reply generation, or requester-resumption contract is defined.

observable: Replies return to the unit that issued each request.

tools.definition: Two one-way channels make a two-way exchange: the requestor sends on a request channel and the replier answers on a separate (usually point-to-point) reply channel; the requestor either blocks until the reply arrives or registers a callback a listener invokes later.

hooks.clause: a subagent handback is the reply leg; design the request and reply records as a pair
the resident's loopback is a request-reply pair over the record streams

tools.title: Synchronous block vs asynchronous callback requestor

transform.reason: No caller suspension and callback-resumption state model is available.

observable: Units wait or continue while requests remain outstanding.

tools.definition: Blocking keeps the code simple and the thread idle; a callback keeps the requestor free but needs a listener thread and state to resume from, which is where correlation and return address become necessary.

hooks.clause: an operator waiting on a run is the blocking requestor; the resident callback model frees attention but needs stored request state

tools.title: Messaging RPC, Messaging Query, Notify/Acknowledge
tools.definition: Three request-reply shapes: a command whose reply is a result document (messaging RPC), a query whose reply is the matching data (messaging query), and an event whose reply merely acknowledges receipt.

hooks.clause: a receipt is the acknowledge leg of notify/acknowledge; name which exchanges need a result instead

tools.title: Return Address

transform.reason: No header-field editing or reply construction transform is defined.

observable: Each response follows the destination named by its request.

tools.definition: The requestor names the channel it wants the reply on in the request header; hard-coding the reply channel in the replier would couple it to the requestor's channel decisions and prevent different requests from being answered in different places.

hooks.clause: a worker should write its result where the dispatch record says, never to a path baked into the worker
hook results carry their destination rather than assuming one

tools.title: Correlation Identifier

transform.reason: No identifier creation, copying, and outstanding-request lookup contract is defined.

observable: Concurrent replies match the correct originating request.

tools.definition: Each request carries a unique request id that the replier copies into the reply as a correlation id, so a requestor with many outstanding requests can match each reply; the pattern names six roles: requestor, replier, request, reply, request id, correlation id.

hooks.clause: every fan-out dispatch carries an id its handback must echo; aggregation depends on it
receipts carry the order or event id they answer

tools.title: Correlation key choice: generated message id vs business key; correlating chains

transform.reason: No key uniqueness, reuse, or cross-hop identity model is supplied.

observable: Replies become ambiguous when unit request keys collide.

tools.definition: A system-generated message id is unique but meaningless to the business, while a business key (order number) is meaningful but may repeat or be absent; across a chain of exchanges the requestor stores request state keyed by the id and each hop preserves or re-derives it.

hooks.clause: the order id is the business correlation key across lifecycle records; a per-dispatch id is the technical one

verified.note: model-knowledge (the site excerpt defers to a separate article)

tools.title: Message Sequence

transform.reason: No payload fragmentation and reassembly transform exists.

observable: Numbered parts reconstruct one unit payload.

tools.definition: Data too large for one message is split into a sequence whose members carry a sequence identifier (which set), a position identifier (order within the set) and a size or end indicator (when the set is complete), so the receiver can reassemble it.

hooks.clause: long worker outputs chunked into records need set id, position and end marker
multi-record evidence appended to the log should carry sequence and end markers

tools.title: Politics and organisation (Conway's law)
tools.definition: Integration crosses business-unit and IT-group boundaries and application ownership shifts over time, so organisational communication structure shapes the technical solution.

place.chapter: Chapter 1: Solving Integration Problems Using Patterns

tools.title: Reassembly, out-of-order parts, and the claim-check alternative

transform.reason: No message-part or external-payload store contract is available.

observable: Buffering and transfer volume differ between two large-data strategies.

tools.definition: The receiver must buffer parts until the end marker arrives and tolerate arrival out of order (a resequencer); when the data need not travel at all, storing it once and sending a claim check avoids the sequence entirely.

hooks.clause: prefer a claim check (path plus hash) over chunking large evidence through the log

verified.note: model-knowledge (the site excerpt stops before reassembly)

tools.title: Message Expiration

observable: Unconsumed messages leave the normal queue after their time limit.

tools.definition: A message carries a time limit beyond which it is useless; an unconsumed message past the limit is treated as never sent, usually by rerouting it to the dead letter channel, sometimes by discarding it.

hooks.clause: time budgets on dispatches: a stale request should expire to a dead-letter record, not run late
beacon age is an expiration judgment made by the reader

tools.title: Expiration mechanics: timestamp vs time-to-live, clock skew, reply expiration

transform.reason: Clock skew and absolute-to-relative deadline conversion require an explicit time model.

observable: Units disagree about expiry when their clocks differ.

tools.definition: Expiry can be an absolute timestamp or a relative time-to-live the system converts at send; absolute times need synchronised clocks; a reply may inherit a shorter deadline than its request because the requestor stops waiting.

hooks.clause: a worker's deadline should be shorter than the operator's wait so the reply is never dead on arrival

verified.note: model-knowledge (the site excerpt omits header and clock details)

tools.title: Format Indicator
tools.definition: A message says which format it uses so receivers can handle format change; three forms: a version number both sides map to a format, a foreign key (file name, row key, URL) pointing at a format document, or the format document itself embedded in the message.

hooks.clause: the beacon codebook versions are the version-number form; every record kind should carry one
exported kits should carry a format indicator so an instance knows which codebook to read with

tools.title: Simple messaging examples (JMS and .NET request/reply, JMS publish/subscribe)
tools.definition: Three small worked examples show the base patterns in code on two platforms: request-reply over JMS, the same over .NET and MSMQ, and the Observer pattern over a JMS publish-subscribe topic.

tools.title: JMS Request/Reply Example
tools.definition: A requestor and replier on JMS queues demonstrate request and reply channels, the return address and correlation id headers, and an invalid-message channel for requests the replier cannot read.

hooks.clause: a minimal probe: send a request record, expect a correlated reply, route garbage to the invalid stream

tools.title: .NET Request/Reply Example
tools.definition: The same request-reply exchange built on .NET and MSMQ, showing the pattern is platform-independent while the API details (queue paths, message properties) differ.

hooks.clause: the same probe should hold across hosts (Claude, Codex, Copilot) with only adapter differences

tools.title: JMS Publish/Subscribe Example (Observer over a topic)

transform.reason: The combined example needs notification payloads, pull replies, and durable subscription state.

observable: Observers receive updates through alternative exchange sequences.

tools.definition: The Observer pattern implemented with a publish-subscribe topic: a subject publishes event messages, observers subscribe; the example compares push and pull notification and shows durable subscriptions and how several subjects and observers share topics.

related.title: Observer over messaging: push vs pull notification

hooks.clause: the board as observer of beacon topics; choose push or pull per record kind

tools.title: Routing taxonomy: simple routers, composed routers, architectural routers
tools.definition: The chapter groups routers into simple ones that make one decision per message (content-based, filter, dynamic, recipient list, splitter, aggregator, resequencer), composed ones built from simple ones (composed message processor, scatter-gather), and architectural ones that shape the whole solution (routing slip, process manager, message broker).

tools.title: Content-Based Router

observable: Message values below a threshold take one destination; other values take the other.

tools.definition: When one logical function lives in several physical systems, the router inspects message content (field presence or values) and sends each message to the channel of the system that should handle it; routing logic must stay easy to maintain, with a rules engine for complex cases.

hooks.clause: the scheduler routes orders to lanes by kind; keep the rule table small and visible
a verdict record routes to repair or to review by its content
